title: Motion to Respond of Towering Concerns, LLC to the Motion for Leave to Answer and Limited Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. filed on 10/01/2026 under ER26-3525.

documents.name: Towering_Concerns_Response_to_the_Response.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA ​
                             BEFORE THE ​
               FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



    Towering Concerns, L.L.C.                                            Docket No. ER26-3525



     MOTION TO RESPOND TO MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND LIMITED
       ANSWER OF PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C. TO THE PROTEST AND
      COMMENTS OF THE TOWERING CONCERNS, LLC RE THE 08/14/2026
          REGARDING FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION ​
                      (FERC) DOCKET NO. ER26-3525



Recognizing that protesting what should be a routine filing is unusual, Towering
Concerns respectfully asks that the Commission consider the following new
information regarding the tariff filing ER26-3525.

Analysis of the data referenced in PJM’s Answer1 has spotlighted many more
discrepancies between the filing and PJM’s planning data. The Answer has also
generated new questions about the cost allocation for project b4000.345, and it has
added to the difficulty the public has in searching for accurate information on the
project.

We respect this process, and we want the Commission and PJM to know we are not
making these filings frivolously.



PJM affirms its filing is inaccurate and out of date
Without insulting the intelligence of the Commissioners, we wish to emphasize for
the record that when PJM directed the Commission to its website to find

1
 Motion for Leave to Answer and Limited Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to the Protest and
Comments of the Towering Concerns, LLC re the 08/14/2026 filing ER26-3525.
 up-to-date project information on b4000.345, it affirmed our claim that ER26-3525
was indeed inaccurate and, according to PJM, also out-of-date2.

Our argument3 is that the tariff should be rejected or deferred because it is
inaccurate. PJM has now affirmed the filing’s inaccuracy, but it made no attempt to
correct the record, instead directing the Commission to do its own research to find
accurate information on PJM projects.



We followed PJM’s invitation to scrutinize cost allocations
and project descriptions
With respect to the Commission's workload, we took it upon ourselves to compare
the 1,761 projects in ER26-3525 with PJM’s website4. The full comparison is attached
to this motion in spreadsheet form. Following is a summary of cost allocation and
project description discrepancies between PJM’s internal documents and the FERC
filing:

Cost Allocation Discrepancies
Table 1 below shows a summary of cost allocation discrepancies in the 1,761 projects
in ER26-3525 Attachment C with PJM’s planning website5.

There are 268 projects in PJM’s planning data with cost allocations that differ from
those provided to the Commission.

PJM noted only 38 projects with cost allocation changes by redline in Attachment C.



2
  PJM said in its motion: “PJM maintains current project information for all projects included in the
PJM RTEP on the Project Status& Cost Allocation page of its website. Additionally, the May 2026
TEAC materials describe the scope change, including the 230 kV underbuild capability, the revised
structure configuration, and the project’s estimated costs.” The referenced website is
https://www.pjm.com/planning/m/project-construction . Please note all of these documents
predate ER26-3525. See Motion for Leave to Answer and Limited Answer of PJM Interconnection,
L.L.C. to the Protest and Comments of the Towering Concerns, LLC re the 08/14/2026 filing ER26-3525.
3
  Protest and Comments of Towering Concerns, LLC requesting FERC to reject or defer PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C.'s 08/14/2026 filing ER26-3525.
4
  We used Claude AI to compare data between PJM’s filing and data downloaded from PJM’s website.
5
  https://www.pjm.com/planning/m/project-construction
 All of the cost allocation discrepancies we found are noted in the spreadsheet in the
yellow column on the spreadsheet under separate attachment as
Discrepancies.xlsx.

Project Description Discrepancies

Our analysis identified more than 800 differences in project descriptions between
the filing and PJM’s planning website. These are noted in Table 1 below. Most of
these are minor discrepancies, such as spelling or abbreviation changes. Although
we are primarily concerned with b4000.345, we note for the record that b4000.324,
b4000.344, b4000.351, b4000.352, b4000.359, b4053.11, b4053.13, and b4068.5 may
also deserve scrutiny regarding cost allocation due to what seems to be significant
scope changes that were not reported to the Commission.

Several other projects include changes that we don’t understand and that we hope
others with expertise will scrutinize.

All of the project description discrepancies we found are noted in the spreadsheet
in the two yellow columns on the spreadsheet under separate attachment as
Discrepancies.xlsx.

 230kV addition to b4000.345 might change the Tariff
Since our analysis identified so many discrepancies, we took time to more carefully
analyze the 230kV supplemental addition to the Kraken. The supplement might
actually require a change to the cost allocation for project b4000.345, because the
230kV line will not service those outside Dominion’s service area.

       The 230 kV line [added to b4000.345 and b4000.344] will be utilized to serve
       approximately 3 GW of requested load6 in the immediate transmission
       corridor. …

       The North Anna to Thornburg to Bristers (formerly Kraken Loop) corridor
       is experiencing significant growth driven by large scale data center
       development. To date, at least ten new Delivery Point (“DP”) requests to serve
       data center load in the corridor have been submitted, in addition to existing
       data center load in the vicinity from Elmont to Fredericksburg. …

       On the Dominion system, 500 kV transmission lines are reserved for bulk
       power transfers while 230 kV facilities (and below) are used to directly serve
       load. Additional facilities to accommodate load‑serving needs and future
       reinforcements associated with the significant data center growth in the
       corridor will be required.7 (emphasis added)

We don’t pretend to be experts, but we do wonder why out of state power
companies are being asked to cover the additional $60 million cost of a 230kV line
that will be utilized by Dominion customers in the immediate transmission



6
  The load has not been “requested,” as more than ten local data center projects in Stafford alone
have not yet been approved. PJM is accepting speculative estimates based on progress of data
center applications that are unknowable. In addition, because it is wasting so much time on data
center applications that don’t pan out, Dominion itself has recently changed its application process,
according to Charlie Payne. The recently downsized Ackokeek data center project in Stafford had no
information on grid connection that it could provide to the planning commission or Board of
Supervisors
(https://www.facebook.com/protectstaffordva/posts/-this-is-the-final-voteaccokeek-center-spea
k-up-october-7the-planning-commission/122195400974900674/) due to Dominion’s new
procedures.
7
 https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/teac/2026/20260602
/20260602-item-11---dom-supplemental-projects.pdf
 corridor? Should the cost allocation alter so Dominion foots its fair share of a bill
for supplemental build out that serves its customer base alone8?



PJM’s new “Thornburg Project”
In its motion, PJM said, “The scope change did not create a new project or replace
the reliability need for which [the 230kV addition] was selected”9, but in that
motion, PJM gave the Kraken Loop its fifth new name, adding to the confusion
about whether it is indeed a new project, making it more challenging for the public
to find information on the project, and underscoring our protest about the common
sense need for accuracy in public filings.

For clarity, what follows is a brief history of the different names PJM and Dominion
have given the Kraken as its proposed scope, location, and terminus have changed:

In 2024 RTEP Window 1, Dominion proposed a new project called the “Kraken
Loop,”10.

In 2025, Dominion briefly renamed the project the “North Anna-Kraken Loop” or
“North Anna-Kraken”11.




8
   We note here that Dominion’s last attempt to add a 230kV line in this corridor resulted in a lawsuit
when out of state power companies argued they shouldn’t have to pay for projects that only
benefited Virginians in a localized area. The lawsuit took many years to complete, and Dominion was
found to be in the wrong. See Old Dominion Electric Cooperative and North Carolina Electric
Membership Corporation v. Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a Dominion Virginia Power,
Docket No. ELI 0-49-000 (FERC Mar. 17, 2010) “On March 20, 2014, FERC issued an Order on
Reserved Issue in which it found that customers outside Virginia should not bear any of the
incremental underground costs, but that Virginia customers in the Dominion zone should share
such costs.” https://rga.lis.virginia.gov/Published/2014/RD420/PDF
9
   Motion for Leave to Answer and Limited Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to the Protest and
Comments of the Towering Concerns, LLC re the 08/14/2026 filing ER26-3525.
10
   https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/teac/2025/2025030
4/20250304-2024-rtep-window-1-reliability-analysis-report.pdf
11
   The Kraken’s second name is noted here as the third name was announced
https://www.facebook.com/StaffordCountyGovernment/posts/dominion-has-again-changed-the-
name-of-the-proposed-transmission-line-project-th/1334358468726151/
 In February 2026, after being mocked in the press and by the public for the
unintentionally ironic name Kraken12 Loop, Dominion renamed the proposed
Kraken substation to the Thornburg substation and renamed the Kraken Loop
project the “North Anna to Bristers” project13.

In July 2026, Dominion announced it had split the project in two, giving b4000.345
a fourth name, the Thornburg to Bristers 500 & 230 kV Transmission Line Project:




12
  A kraken is a mythical sea monster that kills unsuspecting sailors with its long-reaching tentacles.
13
 https://www.facebook.com/StaffordCountyGovernment/posts/dominion-has-again-changed-the
-name-of-the-proposed-transmission-line-project-th/1334358468726151/
  In its September 2026 filing, PJM counsel dubs the project with its fifth moniker,
The “Thornburg Project”.

This new name is especially confusing, since the 230kV line addition proposed for
b4000.345 proposal bypasses the Thornburg substation14 on the route entirely:




It’s unclear how the supplemental application submitted in ER26-3525 will actually
be constructed or funded since as we noted above, b4000.344 and b4000.345 are
being submitted separately to Virginia SCC, and the 230kV addition spans both.

How many substation terminus changes, length changes, splits, and name changes
must a project endure before it becomes ”new”? ​




14

https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/teac/2026/20260602
/20260602-item-11---dom-supplemental-projects.pdf
 By giving project b4000.345 yet a fifth completely new name found in no other
public filing, PJM prevents the public from finding information about b4000.345 /
Kraken Loop / North Anna-Kraken Loop / North Anna to Bristers / Thornburg to
Bristers / Thornburg project.



Help
Again, we respectfully ask the Commission for help. We are ordinary people. We
don’t have lawyers helping us. We just want to be able to find information on
projects that affect us, but PJM’s inaccurate and out-of-date filings coupled with
ever-changing names for existing proposals makes that near impossible. Good
information helps people make good decisions, and without good information,
Staffordians cannot make arguments or decisions about this proposal that will
affect our schools, homes, farms, and families for many generations to come.

We respectfully reiterate our request that the Commission reject or defer
ER26-3525 until PJM submits accurate, consistent project information. We amend
our protest to note the cost allocation inconsistencies found in our comparison of
PJM’s project data with ER26-3525 Appendix C, noting that the Tariff may indeed
include cost allocation errors that necessitate rejection.

Scope and counts				
Projects listed in PDF (scope)	1761			
  …of which found in spreadsheet (compared)	1760

Non-LRS cost allocation differs	269

Load-ratio-share (LRS) cost allocation differs	6			
Marked as redline in PDF (among differing projects)	38			
				
How to read this workbook				
Fields compared	Description and cost allocation (the only project data the PDF contains), matched on project ID.			
Scope	Only projects listed in the PDF. Spreadsheet projects that are not in the PDF were ignored.			
Spreadsheet vs. PDF	Orange = spreadsheet value; green = PDF value; yellow = what changed.			
Description matching	Formatting-only differences are ignored: case, spacing, punctuation, quotes, '#' vs 'No.', 'approx.' vs 'approximately', 'mi.' vs 'miles', etc. Anything left is reported.			
Allocation matching	Percentages compared per customer; differences under 0.005 pt ignored. 'NEPTUNE*' = Neptune; 'MetEd' = ME. PDF 'DFAX' or unlabeled lists = spreadsheet Non-LRS column.			
Redline	The PDF is a redline; colored (underlined) text marks proposed additions. Only 39 projects carry that marking.
